title: Mike Todasco - The Future of Innovation

turns.speaker: Ricardo Pascual
paragraphs: Welcome to the Innovation Conversation, a podcast about innovators, both in business and real life, hosted by myself, Ricardo Pascual, and Harry McGonna. This podcast is also sponsored by Odev Tech. Odev Tech is your premier software development partner. Make sure you check them out at odev.tech. The podcast is also sponsored by notion.so. Notion is offering six months for free for new users. Make sure you check out our website at startup events.co.uk to read more about the software. Hi, and welcome to another episode of the Innovation Conversation. Today we are joined by Mike Todasco. Mike, welcome to the podcast. Ricardo,

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: Thanks for having me. I'm excited about the conversation we're going to have.

turns.speaker: Ricardo Pascual
paragraphs: Pleasure having you here, Mike. Would you like to introduce yourself to the audience, please?

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: Yeah, I'd love to. Hello everyone, Mike Todasco. My background is varied. I started off my career in the world of finance and accounting. I ran my own business for a few years. I joined PayPal, was in products there, worked on some really cool, exciting products in my time there. But then in my second half of my career within PayPal, I ran the innovation group there after we had separated from eBay. Did that for about six years, and then most recently left that to work at a university at an AI center at San Diego State University.

turns.speaker: Ricardo Pascual
paragraphs: Quite an impressive career. It seems like you're the right guy to talk about anything to do with innovation, but also AI, because I was having a look. I'm ready for it, Ricardo. Yeah. Okay, all right. So I think, having that background and coming from PayPal, one of the first questions is, how important is it for a tech company, or something that started as a startup and grew into this tech company like PayPal, to continue to focus on innovation? Look,

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: I think for a technology company, you need to be ahead of the curve. I live very close to where Intel's headquarters are. For anybody who might be following the news on Intel, it was a technology company that birthed so much of what we have today, but they missed mobile, they missed GPUs, they missed so many things. Now it has an ousted CEO, it's a shell of its former self, and that's what happens in technology. If you're not innovating, if you're not up on what the next new thing is going to be, you can still survive, but you're not going to thrive. So for any company in the technology space, you need to be thinking about what are the next platforms, and ultimately, what are the better ways that I can use technology to better serve the customers who I have now or who I want to be my future customers. These are questions that everybody in tech companies, or just about any company, should be asking themselves.

turns.speaker: Ricardo Pascual
paragraphs: What do you think makes companies continue to innovate? Is it leadership, culture? What are the defining things that actually help them?

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: PayPal had a culture of innovation because it was forced into it. Yes, there were some extremely innovative, creative people at the top, like Reed Hoffman and Elon Musk and David Sacks. All these people were founders of PayPal or very early employees, but they definitely created a culture that permeated. There were many things on the risk and security side of PayPal that were being forced into because PayPal as a company in 2000 was doing things that the world had not seen before. One example that I think was an amazing innovation, which sounds so simplistic nowadays, but back in the days when people were trying to add their bank accounts to PayPal, they had to send in to PayPal a paper check that somebody had to actually look at and type in and all this stuff.

It was a total archaic, really difficult process. Somebody suggested, an engineer I believe suggested, what if we had a pin number instead? This led to a thing that's actually still used today in banks in the United States, where often if you want to confirm your bank account, you will get a micro payment. They will send you 16 cents and 34 cents, two random amounts. You type those in, and that's a way that they can actually confirm a bank account. It's way less costly to send a few cents to somebody than it is to have a paper check and this whole process. That was just something that was birthed out of necessity.

So I think a lot of innovation comes down to what's the need, what are you trying to serve, and also having a culture that's going to encourage that. Of course, I'm sure we'll talk more about failure and things like that at some point, but a culture that is not going to, when you screw up, when it doesn't work, when you gave it a good faith effort and tried something, that's not the end of your career. You need to pivot and shake yourself off and learn from that and just move on to something else. How you create a culture that really emphasizes on those types of things, that's pivotal in making an innovative company. Well, I think

turns.speaker: Ricardo Pascual
paragraphs: It just leads to my next question, which is exactly that. How do you manage to create that? Because a lot of people when they're working, they're quite afraid of making mistakes, and then they don't risk, they don't try to do anything new. It's more, okay, I know this works, I'll keep on doing this until it might die in days. But in reality, we all need to adapt, we actually need to grow very quickly. So how do you foster that within the company itself, and how do you promote that sense of it's okay to make mistakes, and actually expect you to make mistakes because that means you're creating something new?

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: Every company is different, and every company needs to find their own way to do that. I think leading by example is a great way to do that for senior leadership. If you only talk to employees about your successes, that is going to be a tell for them that they're not allowed to fail either. When you are a leader and you're very open in your own shortcomings, and you get up on stage and say, hey, we screwed this up, or when you say, I screwed this up as a leader, that's a tell to make it known that hey, it's okay to try stuff. We want to learn from that.

One company that actually inspired us a lot at PayPal was a company called Ben and Jerry's, which for people who might not know, is an ice cream company. One of the things they have at Ben and Jerry's is they have something called a flavor graveyard. At their corporate headquarters, they actually have tombstones for ice cream flavors that have not succeeded, the things that went away and so forth. That's something that their employees can see all the time when they're there as part of that. At PayPal, this was right before COVID, we never actually got to get back to the office and finish it unfortunately, we were actually making a product graveyard.

We were, and it was so great. We had a little model train set with trees and all that. We were kind of recreating the PayPal campus on this scaled down version with little PayPal products or representations of PayPal products with QR codes that you could scan and learn about that. We were interviewing the people who created these things that did not succeed and what they learned from them. Because again, it's not that, look, it's not that you're saying, oh, well, we should just keep failing. No, that's not the point. But failure is a stepping stone to success. You don't go to school or learn a foreign language just expecting, well, yeah, I'm just going to hear it once and I'm going to speak it fluently right back to you and understand.

No, it's an iterative process in how we learn as an individual or as a group. You have to learn from each step, and you're going to get better and better and better as you do that. To just say, I think a lot of companies' natural reaction is, that's a failure, we're never going to talk about that again. That is by far the worst thing that you could possibly be doing.

turns.speaker: Ricardo Pascual
paragraphs: It's interesting you're saying that because I talk to a lot of startups and those investors, and one of the key things that I think investors always look at is, have they been able to pivot? Because they know the first idea is not going to work out, so they're actually looking for the ability to pivot more than anything else. It just goes to show, exactly like you said, you need to continue to innovate, you need to continue making not just mistakes, but being able to take the risk and embrace that risk. It's part of the game, isn't it?

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: There's not been a successful company that exists today that didn't have horror stories, they thought they were going to die, and that didn't have to pivot. Again, to bring up PayPal again, PayPal was a company for wiring money between Palm Pilots. They were using the infrared technology between two Palm Pilot devices to send money, and that's what they were making the whole business about. It just happened to be that Max Levchin, one of the founders, made something as a test where people could send money to an email address. Frankly, from the stories I've heard, the company fought against that. They were kind of like, no, no, that's not what we're about, we're about sending money between Palm Pilots.

All of a sudden, these people started to use this testing thing that Max had set up for sending money to an email address. Then finally, as a company, they had to realize, actually, I guess that's the business. Then it caught on eBay and expanded to all these other things. That was a huge pivot for the company. Again, I don't care what company you are, you have had these stories. It's not always just up and to the right for growth. You are going to have to pivot, you're going to have to, and frankly, you have to listen to your customers. That is the big thing. 99.9% of the time, what you envision as what your customers want is not what they actually need.
You need to really talk to them, understand that, iterate again and again and again until you start to really find that product market fit.

turns.speaker: Ricardo Pascual
paragraphs: When you're leading innovation in such a big company, how do you get that feedback from customers? Sometimes, let's take for example a very recent case, Jaguar, the car company. They completely changed their branding and everyone's kind of against it. The product market fit still remains to be seen, I would say, at this stage. How do you find, within your company, how do you manage to find that?

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: Jaguar's interest, to me, I feel that this is kind of just like a ruse. Again, not to go too far down that path, but it's been fascinating, the rebranding that they've been doing. Because nobody cared about Jaguar before. I don't know what percentage of global car sales they were before this. They were definitely not top of mind. I bet you they weren't in the top 15 car companies. Most people would kind of rattle off or anything. So it's really interesting to generate this and to say, well, we're actually all electric, we're all this now, and we're not about the car anymore, whatever this is. Sometimes, if you were Toyota, you probably would have made that because they're the number one car maker in the world.

But when you're number 15 or whatever Jaguar is, you can take a risk and do something innovative and creative. That was not your question though. Your question, Ricardo, was actually about how do you talk to the customers, how do you get that feedback loop and so forth. I think you need to empower your individual teams more than anything. At PayPal again, we had one team that was focused on charities. The needs of a charity for money and collecting funds and so forth are very different than the needs of a small business that's just an individual, a medium sized business who might have more sophisticated integrations, versus a large business who like a large enterprise.

All of these had different teams focused on them. You need to empower the people in the field to be able to do and build what is best for their own customers. That is the one truth. As a CEO, you can't dictate those things. If you're a five person startup, well, okay, but then you should be the person that's out there talking to the customers, listening, asking questions, and getting to what their problems are. You really want to solve those problems in a way that is innovative, unique, dare I say 10 times better than the way that they're solving their problems today. If you can do those things, then you're going to have a successful product.

The one question to always ask a customer, and this could be as you're investing in a company or whatever else, if your product disappeared today, how would your customers react? If it's not like outright horror and shock, I mean like, oh my gosh, what am I going to do now? Listen to Spotify on the way here. I just got my year in review, my Spotify wrapped. Yeah, there's competing products out there. I love my Spotify. The 20 bucks a month we spend as a family plan, we probably spend 100 bucks a month for easy. I also grew up in the 1990s where CDs used to cost like $17, so it's ridiculous to me how cheap music is nowadays.

But given all that, that's a product that has clearly found fit with their customers, they've built a loyalty and so forth as part of that, even though there are Apple Music and other competing services out there. They do it much more elegantly, and they know your customer. Those are the type of experiences that you need to be able to strive for.

turns.speaker: Ricardo Pascual
paragraphs: We kind of touched upon something interesting, which is getting feedback and therefore learning from your customers. Now I want to make the jump to AI, to AI, because I know you're very passionate and vocal about it. How do you see this whole AI evolution? Is it like a massive threat that we should all hide underneath our beds or something, or actually should embrace it and just stick it to

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: The end? I think the answer is we need to embrace it. Maybe we should be hiding under our beds, I don't know actually. I actually don't know how this is all going to play out. Again, I've already kind of teased my age here, but I started school in the 90s in college, and I had never used the internet before getting to school. I happened to be lucky enough to go to University of Illinois, and the first time I went to school there as a freshman, day one, in the computer labs, there are these browsers and these blue links, and you click on things and it takes you places.

I felt like I just had entered the future when I was there. I went back home to tell my friends about it over the holidays and everything, and they were like, what are you talking about? It wasn't, and of course that played out and that's very much the world we're living in now. What we're seeing in AI is so much bigger than the connectivity I think that we've had from the internet. For so many years when I was at PayPal, there were brilliant machine learning engineers there. They were doing amazing things with the amount of data that we have, with natural language processing, with all these different aspects of the broader world of artificial intelligence.

I'm not an engineer by trade, as I started, I was a finance and accounting guy going way back when, so I could never do the things that they did. But fast forward to today, and you have the most powerful models in the world that the world has ever seen that you can talk to in natural language, either by typing or literally by voice, and you can use these tools for 20 bucks a month. It is just mind blowing at the amount of power that we have. I think people who are really into it, like myself, are seeing how it changes our workflows, things that we do with our families, and just our lives in general.

The rest of the world hasn't fully caught on. I mean, I think ChatGPT or OpenAI has said ChatGPT is like up to 300 million users now on there, but that still is what, 4% of the world's population or something like that? It's still a tiny number if you consider over half of the world is online. So most people are not using these tools. I think you are going to see the tools continue to improve, I do believe that's going to happen. And I do think even more than that, we're going to figure out even more how we could use these tools more effectively. We're going to learn from each other.

Even if the tools didn't improve today, there's so much more gain that we have in front of us. So what that means is, they're not taking our jobs yet. Could they? Possibly, yeah. More likely though is our jobs are going to evolve, and they're going to greatly evolve and greatly change. Just like if you are doing things, if you're a salesperson and it's 1996, let's say, and you've said, oh, my job's not going to change at all over the next 10 years, well, you would have been very wrong about that. Because you're probably doing a lot more email, you're probably doing a lot more this, or whatever else as part of that process.

If you're in sales today, I think the human experience, the one-on-one connection, does matter. But you can have an AI that's listening in on your sales calls and evaluating you on how you're doing your performance so you can improve that. You can have it updating your CRM automatically based on the notes for those calls or whatever it might be. There's just so many different use cases. I think what's important for all of us is to stay on top of this within our personal lives, within our business lives, to just really embrace the tools that are out there. Know that they're going to change, know that they're going to improve.

Even today, I think no matter what your job is, if you just spent three, four, five hours with these tools, you could really start to uncover, oh my gosh, I didn't know that that was possible. I used to do things this way, now I can do things this way. That is going to be essential for anybody who's out there to really stay on top of this, to make sure, yeah, my job is going to evolve, my job is not going to just go away when these models.

turns.speaker: Ricardo Pascual
paragraphs: I read somewhere about a comparison, and that was when cars were invented, and how in 20 years, again, it was a slower adoption, everyone went from having a horse and carriage to having a car, or thinking about having a car. Of course, with the move from one industry to the other, you had a lot of jobs that just disappeared. You don't have that many saddle makers, you don't have that many people putting horseshoes onto horses because you don't have the need. But you do have the transformation of those industries into becoming mechanics. Maybe now they're selling tires instead of selling horseshoes. I agree with you, I think that's probably what's going to happen. We're going to have a lot of transformation, but positive transformation. People will continue being people, so that's probably not going to change.

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: I mean, I was talking to somebody about this just recently, or using the example of McDonald's. So what does McDonald's look like 20, 30 years from now? Who's employed at a McDonald's? Is it nobody? I don't think it's nobody. The concept of ATM machines, which was introduced in the 1970s, people thought bank tellers' jobs are done. turns.speaker: Ricardo Pascual
paragraphs: It's just about the knowledge and access to it, not just access to information, but the ability to process information and actually action information as well. turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: In my workflow, I write a lot and I constantly am using it for writing. turns.speaker: Ricardo Pascual
paragraphs: Cultivate that, not just from schools, but in your professional career. How do you cultivate the thinking, the ability to actually think about a problem and manage to fix it without just saying, this is what I was taught in school so it always works?
